messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
Kaimana Leilani was sixty-seven years old, a widower of three years living alone in the green hills above Honolulu, when he finally sat down in a therapist’s office. He had spent most of his adult life as an interior designer, known for his ability to transform cramped studio apartments into spaces that felt open and breathable. That skill had taken him abroad two and a half years ago, to assist on the renovation of a boutique hotel in Jeddah. He had been in the country less than a week when he was taken.

The men came in the middle of the night, shouting orders in Arabic that Kaimana could not understand. He was bundled into a car, blindfolded, and driven for hours. When the blindfold came off, he was in a small concrete room, maybe eight feet by ten, with a single bare bulb and no windows. For twenty-three days he was held there. The men who guarded him spoke little English; most of what Kaimana heard was rapid, angry Arabic. They shouted at him regularly—demands he could not answer, threats he could only guess at. He learned to keep his voice flat, his answers minimal, his body utterly still. The room became his whole world: the damp smell of the mattress, the click of the lock, the sound of his own breathing. He was released when his family’s ransom was paid, flown home with nothing but the clothes on his back.

Back in Honolulu, Kaimana tried to return to his life. He had lost his wife to cancer two years before the kidnapping, and the home he now occupied was full of her absence as well as his own. He told himself he was fine. He took a small redesign job for a widow in Makiki and found, to his horror, that he could not walk into her spare bedroom without his heart slamming against his ribs. He needed his back to a wall, always—he would scan a room the moment he entered, identifying the exits, positioning himself so that no one could approach from behind. His body reacted before his mind could catch up: a raised voice in a café, a door slamming in a neighbour’s apartment, and he was already flooded with adrenaline, chest tight, hands shaking, before he even registered what had happened.

He began to rehearse every conversation in advance. A phone call with a client, even a routine check-in, would require an hour of preparation: he would write down possible questions the client might ask, script his own responses, run through the exchange aloud until it felt safe. But nothing felt safe. He could not explain to anyone why he had stopped taking on new projects; when he tried to tell a longtime colleague what had happened, he lost the thread mid-sentence, forgot the word for “captive,” and hung up without finishing. The memories came without warning—a sudden flash of the concrete ceiling, and with it the sound of shouting, the syllables sharp and foreign and terrifying in his head. At other times he would recall the event but feel absolutely nothing, as if he were watching a stranger on a screen, numb and detached.

The avoidance grew. He stopped going to his office entirely, then declined all new work. Enclosed spaces became impossible: he could not ride the elevator in his own building, could not sit in the back seat of a car, could not step inside a restroom stall that did not have a door he could prop open. His daughter, who lived two islands away, began to notice his isolation. She asked why he was barely leaving the house. He said he was tired. He was, in truth, terrified—not of being taken again, exactly, but of feeling trapped. Vulnerable. The feeling was unbearable.

What finally brought Kaimana to seek help was a phone call from a client he had known for thirty years. She wanted to hire him for a large project—a custom home in Puna. Kaimana heard himself say yes because he could not find a reason to refuse that did not sound insane. The moment he hung up, he felt a wave of dread that left him curled on his sofa for an hour. He understood then that he was losing more than his business. He was losing the ability to be in the world at all. When his daughter flew over for the weekend, he let her make the appointment. He came to the first session still not sure what he hoped for—only that he was tired of rehearsing a life he was too frightened to live.
